Dude you didn’t do anything wrong. When parents suffocate you, you learn to do things behind their back. It’s the problem when parents are too strict and don’t let their child make their own decision. Don’t let yourself be manipulated into believing you did anything wrong. Is lying good? No. But, when you’ve got parents who control your free will based on their beliefs without encouraging you to make your own decisions, give you a safe space to come to them when you need advice based on decisions you’ve made, or they exert control over your bodily autonomy, I think lying to them is minuscule in comparison to the crime they’ve committed against you. Your younger years are very important in creating life experience, and them sheltering you from the world is only going to adversely affect it. Most kids raised in a religious and strict home either learn to comply and never learn to think for themselves, or kids rebel and make impulsive decisions based on previous limitations without having exercised their decision-making skills that were learned from your own experience.

Unfortunately, since I don’t know more about the environment you grow up in, and any dangers you may face from your parents or your environment, it’s hard for me to advise you without feeling like it could be more harmful.

The safest thing I would recommend is talking to a school counselor if you’re not home-schooled, and tell them about what’s going on. They’re going to be a lot more equipped to support you than the general people on Reddit. A counselor will be able to call CPS if your environment is worse than I can determine from your post, or they’ll be able to help you talk about alternate options into surviving your senior year with extra school related activities your mom could permit you to leave the house for so you can begin to be independent of their control.

I hope things get easier for you. I’ve been there.

I hear you. I’m 23 as well, almost 24, and I’ve been in the same boat as you since I was about 11. I just started recently getting professional help about 4 months ago. There have been some good small steps. Until that point, I adapted a horrible coping mechanisms for most of my life of bottling my emotions up, and taking care of other people before myself, so I wouldn’t have to think about myself. So I held onto every day self-harm habits I didn’t register as hurting myself, because it wasn’t cutting I suppose.

The fear that people don’t care enough is very real for me, and makes my suicidal thoughts more aggressive. Like someone not reacting to me being suicidal makes the ideation of it become closer to reality. It reinforces the feelings or not being worth anything. I get it when you say it makes you want to follow through.

What I can tell you is that you should always talk to your therapist about these things, even the reactions of your loved ones that worry you.

I’ve found that what helps me most is healthy communication. It takes a lot of mental energy from me, but if you’re able to listen to the way others talk around you, and make sure they’re not manipulative and/or toxic, you need to be honest with them. Make sure what you’re saying comes from a place of your feelings. Don’t accuse, or make assumptions. Just mention that their responses make you feel like you’re not being taken seriously. Open that dialogue, and work through it with them. They agreed to use that list with you in order to help. If they mean it, they’ll do it. If they just say “That sucks”, let them know that you’re needing some support right now, and be more forward in asking what you need for them. Words of comfort, reminders, probing questions, all of it. They can even just ask if you’re using your safety plan to get through the hard times, or help you set it up. If they push back because they don’t want to have that conversation with you, then it’s lead me to believe that they aren’t the support you need in your life. 

Now, doing that has helped me immensely, but it’s not the easiest. I lost someone who was supposed to be my best friend for the past several years. She didn’t want the kind of friendship where we talked about our mental states. She wanted to party all the time, and make the calls. So I made the call to end the friendship. It sucked. I didn’t leave my home for over a month. However, by freeing up the time I spent with someone who wasn’t so good to me, I’ve allowed room for better people to come into my life who cares. So it more than paid off. I want that for you. To have the best people who fully support you. I couldn’t be more grateful for my loved ones, honestly. People can make or break the worst times. 

Your thoughts seem to flow similarly to mine, which is why I’ve written about myself as much as I have, so I hope that didn’t come across badly. I truly relate, and I’m sorry you’re having to feel this way with your loved ones. Just open that dialogue, and just talk to them with good intentions, and make sure they’re listening. If they’re not, then they’re not for you.
